extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and researchers in media/cultural studies and broadcast practitioners interested in communication theory
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Stuart Hall's encoding/decoding model to analyze how televisual messages are produced, circulated, decoded, and reproduced, paying attention to codes, institutional power, and audience positions. Useful for media researchers, cultural studies students, and critical analyses of TV/newscasts/advertising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-stage communication circuit
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication consists of four linked but distinctive moments: production, circulation, distribution/consumption (use), and reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the communicative process as a circuit or structure of moments rather than a linear sender/message/receiver chain; each moment is necessary to the whole but retains distinctiveness and its own modalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative autonomy of stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Each stage (production, circulation, consumption, reproduction) is 'relatively autonomous'—coding does not transparently determine reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that what occurs at production fully guarantees reception; analyze the specific determining limits and possibilities at each stage and how they may interrupt continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex structure of dominance
rubrics_metrics.description: Messages have a 'complex structure of dominance' because at each stage they are imprinted by institutional power relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how institutional, political and ideological power shapes sign-vehicles at production, circulation and reception; look for how dominant orders are reproduced through the circuit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizability/appropriateness requirement for reception
rubrics_metrics.description: A message can only be received if it is recognizable or appropriate to the receiving context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether encoded messages fit the code/expectations of target audiences; consider limits on possible uses/interpretations imposed by codes and situational factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Message form / discursive transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: A raw event must be transposed into a 'message form' (discursive story) before it can function as a communicative event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how events are translated into televisual discourse (storying, selection, formal rules) and how this transposition mediates social/political consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production constructs the message
rubrics_metrics.description: Production is the point where the programme/message is constructed, involving material instruments, social production relations, professional ideologies, technical skills and audience assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a programme, map the production practices, institutional structures, professional codes, and resources that shape the encoded message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discursive circulation and distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The discursive form is the medium through which a product circulates and is distributed to different audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace how discourse enables circulation and how distribution practices (formats, channels) shape access and potential readings by varied audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-translation into social practices (reproduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the circuit to complete and have effect, the discourse must be translated into social practices; if meaning is not taken up in practice, it has no effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether and how decoded meanings enter social practice or consciousness and produce influence, instruction, persuasion or entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encoding/decoding correspondence is constructed
rubrics_metrics.description: Correspondence between encoding and decoding is not natural or automatic but constructed; degrees of symmetry/asymmetry determine understanding and distortion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the relation between producers' codes and audience codes rather than assuming transparent transmission; identify points of fit and misfit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operation of codes (coding and naturalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: All signs operate through codes; some codes become naturalized (habitual, apparently 'given') but are cultural conventions rather than transparent representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the specific codes in operation, including those so habitual they appear natural, and analyze how they shape perception and obscure their own constructedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Televisual signicity (aural + visual; iconic but coded)
rubrics_metrics.description: The televisual sign combines visual and aural discourse; it is iconic (appears to possess properties of the thing represented) yet remains coded and cannot be identical with referent reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In visual analysis, avoid equating apparent fidelity with transparency; interrogate the coding operations that produce the sense of realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denotation and connotation as analytic tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish analytically between denotation (literal, near-universal aspects of a sign) and connotation (associative, variable meanings) while recognizing most signs combine both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use denotation/connotation to separate relatively fixed literal meanings from associative ideological meanings; do not reify the analytic distinction as a factual split in discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotation as the site of ideological work
rubrics_metrics.description: Connotative (associative) meanings are where ideological interventions and transformations are most active; this is also where polysemy is exploited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus analysis of ideology on connotative layers—how signs are positioned, framed and associated to broader cultural meanings and 'maps of meaning'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polysemy versus pluralism and hierarchy of connotative codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Polysemy (multiple potential meanings) is not the same as pluralism; connotative codes are not equal—they are organized into dominant, preferred readings within a cultural order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing multiple readings, identify which readings are institutionally preferred or dominant and which are marginalized; do not assume all readings are equally empowered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping events into discursive domains (preferred readings)
rubrics_metrics.description: New or troubling events are assigned to discursive domains (maps of social reality) so they can 'make sense'; cultures impose preferred readings with institutionalized classifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how events are classified, the domains to which they are mapped, and the institutional/logical resources that make certain interpretations 'preferred'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive/practical work of broadcasters (enforcing readings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcasters and producers perform interpretive work—rules of competence and logics-in-use—that actively enforce or prefer one semantic domain over another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate production practices (framing, selection, presentation) that nudge audiences toward particular connotative configurations; treat these as purposeful practices rather than neutral formatting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional code distinctiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: A professional code (metacode) exists that applies technical and presentational criteria; it is relatively independent but often reproduces hegemonic definitions by foregrounding technical values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate professional norms (visual quality, presentational values, 'professionalism') from overtly political/hegemonic codes and examine how professional practices may nonetheless reproduce dominant meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three hypothetical decoding positions
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three ideal-typical decoding positions: dominant-hegemonic (accepts preferred reading), negotiated (accepts general legitimacy but adapts locally), and oppositional (recognizes encoding but decodes contrary to intended meaning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify audience readings using these positions as heuristic categories; test empirically and refine—they are hypotheses about likely decoding strategies, not exhaustive categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematically distorted communication and selective perception critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Misunderstandings are often 'systematically distorted' rather than random; selective perception explanations are insufficient because audience readings show clustered patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating audience responses, look for patterned clusters of interpretation and the structural reasons for distortion rather than attributing variance solely to individual differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject simple behaviourism in audience research
rubrics_metrics.description: Content and audience effects cannot be understood in purely behavioural terms; the semiotic paradigm reveals discursive and ideological structures underlying reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design audience research that attends to codes, discursive frames and ideological work rather than only measuring behavioural inputs/outputs (e.g., recall, isolated effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: No degree zero in language
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no unmediated or purely natural representation; naturalism/realism are effects of specific articulations of language on the real.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid analyses that assume any representation is free from coding; interrogate the articulations that create the appearance of naturalness.
